subject: 오라토리오와 무대 없는 극
title: Drama sung without scenery or acting
content: An oratorio tells a story through soloists, chorus, and orchestra, and it does so without costume, staging, or action. Singers stand and sing, a narrator carries what would otherwise be shown, and the audience constructs the events entirely from what it hears. Understanding why the form developed this way explains several of its features. Its origins were partly practical. Theatrical performance was restricted during certain seasons in several countries, and composers who wanted to write dramatic music during those periods produced works that were dramatic in every respect except staging. The restriction ended and the form survived, which indicates that it had found something worth keeping. The chorus carries far more weight than in staged opera. Without scenery to establish place or crowds to fill a stage, the chorus becomes the crowd, the commentary, and frequently the principal voice, so composers wrote choral movements of a scale and complexity that staged works rarely attempt. Amateur choral societies grew around exactly this repertoire. Narration solves what staging would have shown. A singer reports what happened between the dramatic scenes, which lets the work move across long spans of time without any transition, and this frees the composer to set only the moments worth setting. A staged work must account for everything in between. The absence of spectacle changes the listening. An audience that cannot watch attends to the text and to the music, and performers report that the form is unforgiving because nothing distracts from either. Several composers who wrote for both stage and concert platform described the second as the harder discipline, since a passage that would carry visually must carry on its own. Choirs took up the form and kept it alive. Amateur singers in towns across several countries met weekly to work through these scores, and for many of them it was the only large music they ever performed. That habit sustained the repertoire long after the courts that first paid for it were gone.

subject: 문인 화가와 직업 화가
title: Painting as an accomplishment and as a trade
content: East Asian traditions drew a sharp line between painters who worked for a living and those who painted as one of several skills expected of an educated person. The line was social before it was one of taste, and it produced two bodies of work judged by different standards. The educated amateur painted without payment. Their subjects were few — landscape, bamboo, plum, now and then a friend — their material was ink on paper, and their work was given away rather than sold, so the whole practice sat outside any market. Writing, poetry, and calligraphy accompanied painting as branches of one cultivation. Professionals painted what was commissioned. Court painters, workshop masters, and jobbing hands made portraits, screens, records of ceremonies, and religious images, often in colour on silk, and their skill was far higher in just the areas that training builds. They signed less often and were paid. Criticism favoured the amateurs explicitly. The writings that shaped the tradition were produced by educated men who painted, and they held that work made for money necessarily lacked the quality they valued, which was an untroubled expression of the maker's character. Technical polish was treated as evidence against a painting. The distinction obscured a great deal. Several celebrated amateurs painted constantly and accepted gifts that functioned as payment, several professionals were educated men who lost their positions, and the surviving evidence shows considerable movement between the categories. Modern scholarship treats the division as a claim made by one group about its own standing rather than as a description of who actually painted what. The gap shows in what survives. Works by paid painters were kept by the households that bought them, while ink sheets given between friends were passed on, lost, or worn out, so the record we have is skewed. Any account of who painted what must allow for that.

subject: 도자 무역과 취향의 이동
title: Pottery shipped across oceans and the taste it changed
content: Pots travelled further than almost any other trade good because they survive burial, resist damp, and break rather than rot. Wrecks, middens, and palace inventories across four continents therefore record a trade that reshaped what people in distant places considered beautiful. Production responded to distant markets. Kilns in one country made vessels in shapes nobody there used, decorated with motifs specified by foreign buyers, in quantities that domestic demand could not have absorbed, so a substantial part of a tradition's output was designed for people its makers never met. Surviving order records specify dimensions and patterns. Buyers adapted what arrived. Imported vessels were mounted in metal, cut down, drilled, and used for purposes their makers had not intended, and households displayed them as evidence of reach rather than using them as tableware. Paintings of European interiors show such pieces arranged for display well before anybody there could make them. Imitation followed and took a century. Attempts to copy imported porcelain failed again and again because the body needed clays and heat that local potters lacked, and the eventual success took spying, prospecting, and money from the state. The intervening imitations in earthenware form a distinct tradition of their own. Taste moved in both directions. Motifs invented for export returned home as fashion, colours preferred abroad were adopted domestically, and by the eighteenth century it is frequently impossible to say whether a design originated with the makers or the buyers. What the trade produced was a shared visual vocabulary across regions that had almost nothing else in common. Broken pots tell us most of it. A shard keeps its glaze and its clay body for centuries in the ground, so kiln sites and rubbish heaps let us date and place what a written record never noted. Whole vessels in museums are the rare part of the story.

subject: 꼭두각시극의 구조
title: A puppet play carried in a box
content: Travelling puppet traditions had to fit into what a company could carry, and that constraint determined the form as completely as any dramatic convention. The stage folds, the figures pack into a chest, and the whole apparatus is set up in an hour on any level ground. The screen conceals the operators. A cloth or wooden barrier at waist height hides those working below while the figures appear above it, so the audience sees only the puppets, and the operators work by feel and by long habit rather than by watching. This arrangement means a performance can be given wherever a frame can be erected. The figures are simple by necessity. Carved heads on sticks, with jointed arms controlled by rods or strings, must survive transport, be repaired on the road, and read from a distance, so features are exaggerated and colours strong. A company carried a fixed cast that appeared in every play, which is why the same characters recur across the repertoire. Voices are supplied by one or two performers. A single operator speaks for several figures, distinguishing them by pitch and manner, and audiences accept the convention immediately, so a cast of a dozen can be performed by three people including the musicians. The plays are episodic. Scenes are joined loosely rather than built into a single plot, which allows a performance to be lengthened or shortened according to the audience, and permits episodes to be dropped when a figure breaks. Every feature of the form follows from the fact that the whole theatre had to travel on somebody's back. The audience sat close and joined in. Children shouted warnings to the figures, adults called back at the rude ones, and the player answered from behind the cloth, so the show was an exchange rather than a display. That is hard to stage in a modern theatre.

subject: 가사라는 긴 노래
title: A poetic form with no fixed length
content: A Korean verse form consists of paired phrases in a fixed metre repeated for as long as the subject requires. Unlike forms that specify a number of lines, this one specifies only the internal rhythm, so a work may run to twenty lines or to several hundred, and the length is determined by content rather than by convention. The metre is simple and relentless. Each line divides into two halves with a set number of syllable groups, and the pattern continues without variation, which makes the form easy to compose in and easy to memorise. Writers used it for material that resists compression: journeys, exile, seasonal rounds, instruction, and complaint. Its openness suited description. A traveller recording a route, a wife describing a household year, or an official narrating a posting could continue as long as the material lasted, and the resulting works read as accumulation rather than as argument. Nothing in the form pushes toward a conclusion. Authorship was unusually wide. Court officials wrote in the form, and so did women in domestic settings whose compositions circulated in manuscript among relatives, and so did anonymous authors whose works survive in copies. That range makes the surviving body of work a source for voices that formal literature excluded. It was sung rather than read aloud. Performance stretched the syllables considerably, so a work that takes minutes to read occupied a much longer span, and the metre served the singing before it served the page. Recordings made in the twentieth century preserve the practice, and reading such a work silently gives a poor sense of what it was. Manuscript copies kept the form alive. Households wrote out works they liked, passed the books between kin, and added their own, so a great deal survives that no printer ever handled. Those copies are now the main source for what women in such homes actually wrote.

subject: 잡지 표지의 전략
title: The page that has to sell what is behind it
content: A magazine cover competes on a rack with dozens of others, is seen for a moment by somebody who has not decided to buy anything, and must communicate what the publication is before conveying what this issue contains. The conventions that developed are precise and largely invisible to readers. The top third carries the identity. Because covers overlap on display, the upper portion may be all that shows, so the title sits there and never moves, and designers who relocate it are told by circulation figures that they were wrong. The logotype changes rarely and slightly. A single dominant image does the work. Covers built around one photograph or illustration outperform assemblages, since the eye resolves one image at a distance and a collection of small ones at arm's length, and publications that use several elements are addressing subscribers rather than newsstand buyers. Cover lines are hierarchical. One line is set large and the others small, so a reader receives the main proposition first and the rest as supporting evidence, and the writing of these lines is a specialised craft — short, concrete, and promising something specific rather than describing a topic. Eyes matter more than any other element. Covers showing a face looking directly outward perform measurably better, which publishers established by testing and have relied on since, and the effect appears across cultures and categories. Digital display reversed several of these rules. A cover seen as a thumbnail must survive extreme reduction, so recent designs use fewer lines, larger type, and simpler images, and the racks that shaped the older conventions have largely disappeared from the calculation. The rack has largely gone. Most copies are now sold by post or read on a screen, so the design problem that shaped the form for a century has changed shape, and covers are being redrawn for a display the size of a stamp.

subject: 화면 배치의 위계
title: Arranging a page so that the eye knows where to go
content: Any designed surface presents several things at once, and the viewer cannot attend to them simultaneously. Establishing which element is seen first, which second, and which only when sought is the central problem of layout, and the tools available for solving it are few and well understood. Size does most of the work. The largest element is seen first, and a design in which everything is the same size has no order at all, so a designer establishes rank by making the differences decisive rather than slight. Elements close in size compete and produce hesitation. Contrast against the surroundings ranks what size does not. A small element in strong colour against a quiet field will be seen before a large one that matches its background, so weight, colour, and isolation all substitute for scale. Isolation is the strongest and the least used, since giving something space costs space. Position exploits reading habit. In a tradition that reads from one corner, the eye enters there by default, so an element placed at that corner is found without effort while one placed at the opposite corner must be made prominent to compete. Designs for traditions reading in another direction invert this exactly. Alignment creates the invisible structure. Elements sharing an edge read as related, and a page in which everything aligns to a small number of lines feels organised even where the viewer cannot say why, which is why grids underlie almost all professional layout. The reader never sees the grid and always sees its absence. None of this is noticed when it works. A reader who finds a page easy has been guided through it by choices they never saw, and one who finds a page hard is usually looking at a layout with no order at all. Good work here is invisible by design.

subject: 상차림의 순서
title: How dishes are arranged on a table
content: Traditions that serve many dishes at once must decide where each goes, and the arrangements are prescribed rather than casual. What sits nearest the diner, what sits at the far edge, and what occupies the centre all follow rules that members of the tradition follow without thinking about them. Reach determines the basic order. Items eaten from constantly sit within easy reach, items shared sit between diners, and items taken occasionally sit further away, so the layout is a map of expected frequency. A dish placed wrongly is noticed because reaching for it disrupts the meal. Temperature governs the rest. Hot dishes are placed where they will be eaten soonest, cold ones can wait, and a soup that must stay warm sits close to the diner rather than in the middle, which is why the arrangements differ between traditions serving hot and cold food together. Number carries meaning. Several traditions count the side dishes and name the meal by that count, so the arrangement announces the occasion and the household's means before anybody eats. Formal meals prescribe both the number and which categories must be represented. Service style determines everything else. Where each diner receives a full set, the arrangement repeats at every place; where dishes are shared from the centre, the individual place holds only rice and utensils. The two systems produce entirely different tables and different manners, and traditions that shifted from one to the other did so within living memory in several countries. Documentation exists in manuals and in paintings, which frequently disagree with each other about what an ordinary meal looked like. Photographs settle arguments about this. Painted and photographed meals from earlier periods show arrangements that written manuals do not match, so what people actually put on a table differed from what the books said they should. Both records are worth having.

subject: 잔치 음식의 규모
title: Cooking for two hundred people without a kitchen
content: A village feast for a wedding or a funeral required feeding everybody who came, which might be several hundred people, using domestic equipment and no refrigeration. The arrangements that made this possible were as organised as any commercial operation and left almost no written record. Neighbours supplied the labour. Households sent people according to obligations that everybody tracked, and the work was divided by task and by skill, so one group prepared vegetables while another managed fires and a third served. The record of who helped was remembered and repaid at the next occasion. Equipment was borrowed. Large pots, bowls, tables, and mats circulated between households for exactly these events, kept by whoever had storage and produced when needed, and in many communities the set belonged to the village rather than to anybody. Its condition was a collective concern. Menus were built around what could be made in quantity. Dishes requiring individual attention were excluded, preparations that improve after standing were favoured, and the whole sequence was planned so that items could be finished in waves rather than simultaneously. This is the same logic that governs any large kitchen. Timing was the hardest part. Guests arrived across many hours, so food had to be produced continuously rather than at once, and those managing the cooking made judgements about pace with no way to know how many would come. The system depended on people who had done it many times. Commercial catering replaced it within a generation in most places, and communities that remember the older arrangement describe losing the assembly rather than the food. Somebody had to wash up as well. Hundreds of bowls came back dirty with no running water, and that work fell to the same neighbours who had cooked, which is the part of such occasions that nobody records and everybody remembers.

subject: 우물과 공동 공간
title: The well as the centre of a settlement
content: Before piped supply, a settlement was organised around wherever water could be drawn. The well determined where houses were built, how far people walked daily, and where they encountered each other, so its position shaped the community's form and its social life together. Distance set the layout. Carrying water is heavy work done several times a day, so dwellings clustered within a tolerable radius, and settlements that grew beyond that radius either sank another well or divided into neighbourhoods around separate ones. Maps of old villages show this clustering clearly. Ownership and access were governed carefully. A well might belong to a household, to a group, or to the settlement, and the rules about who could draw, when, and in what order were understood by everybody and occasionally litigated, since a dispute about water is a dispute about survival. Maintenance obligations were shared. The site became a meeting place by necessity. People arrived at predictable times, waited, and talked, so news circulated there, and for members of the community whose movement was otherwise limited this was the principal occasion on which they met others. Ethnographers studying such settlements identified the well alongside the laundry site as the main channel of information. Ritual attached to it. Many traditions marked the first drawing of the year, made offerings at the well, and observed prohibitions about what could be brought near, which reflects both practical concern for contamination and the recognition that everything depended on it. Where piped water arrived, the structure frequently remained as a marker long after it stopped being used, and several such wells are now preserved as monuments to an arrangement that nobody would choose to return to. Depth mattered as much as position. A shallow well ran dry in a bad summer and a deep one cost more to sink than most villages could raise, so the choice of site was a wager about weather that a whole settlement lived with for generations.

subject: 연날리기의 구조
title: A frame, a skin, and a length of string
content: A kite flies because air deflected downward by an inclined surface pushes it up, and every traditional design solves the same set of problems: keeping the surface at the right angle, keeping it stable, and keeping it light enough to rise. Traditions across many countries arrived at overlapping solutions. The frame determines the shape and most of the weight. Split bamboo dominates wherever it grows, since it is light, strong along its length, and bends without breaking when heated, and the number and arrangement of spars distinguishes regional types. A frame too heavy will not rise and one too light collapses in wind. The bridle sets the angle. Lines attached at two or more points on the frame meet at a knot where the flying line is tied, and moving that knot changes the angle at which the kite meets the air, so a flier adjusts it according to wind strength. This adjustment is the main skill, and it is done by feel. Stability is achieved by tail or by shape. A tail adds drag behind the centre and keeps the kite pointing into the wind; alternatively a curved or dihedral surface achieves the same without a tail, which permits the manoeuvrable designs used in fighting traditions. The two approaches produce different flying behaviour entirely. Fighting kites remove the tail deliberately. Traditions in several countries fly kites that can be steered by pulling the line, with abrasive-coated string used to cut an opponent's line, and the resulting contests draw large crowds. What began as a toy became, in those places, a sport with its own craftsmen and its own seasons. Seasons governed when they flew. Many traditions fly at one time of year, tied to a festival or to the winds, so the craft is practised in bursts and the rest of the year is spent making. Children learn by helping with that making.

subject: 오방색의 배치
title: Placing five colours where they belong
content: A scheme naming five colours and assigning each to a direction governs where they appear in traditional East Asian decoration. The scheme is not a palette in the modern sense, since it prescribes placement as much as selection, and objects made under it record a geometry rather than a taste. Directional assignment determines architecture. In painted buildings each colour occupies the position its direction assigns, so a viewer who knows the scheme can predict what appears where, and departures from it were noticed. The colours are not distributed for balance; they are distributed according to a map. Ceremonial dress follows the same logic. Garments worn for particular occasions use the colour that the occasion's associations require, and the resulting combinations look arbitrary to an outsider while being fully determined for a participant. Records specify these assignments in detail. Layered combination carries further meaning. Bands of the five colours arranged in sequence appear on sleeves, on ribbons, and on ceremonial objects, and the order in which they are layered is prescribed, so a stripe pattern encodes a statement rather than a decorative rhythm. Children's clothing in several traditions uses exactly this. Protective function was attributed to the arrangement. The combination was held to repel harm, which is why it appears on objects associated with beginnings — a child's first garment, a new building, an occasion marking a change — and the practice persisted long after the cosmology that explained it had faded. Contemporary use is largely aesthetic and it retains the placements. Designers working with the palette follow the traditional positions even when they do not hold the beliefs, which is how a system of thought survives as a visual convention. Cheap dyes changed what was possible. Once bright colours could be bought rather than made, the scheme could be followed exactly by anybody, and what had marked rank became available to all, which weakened the very distinctions it had drawn.

subject: 기념 사진의 구도
title: Arranging a group so that everybody is visible
content: A commemorative group photograph must show every face, indicate who is important, and be made quickly with people who are not accustomed to being arranged. The conventions that solved this problem are consistent across countries and have barely changed in a century. Rows solve visibility. People are placed in tiers — seated, standing, and standing on something — so that no head is hidden, and the arrangement is built from the centre outward. A photographer works quickly because a group holds its arrangement for a limited time before somebody moves. The centre carries rank. The most senior person sits at the middle of the front row, with the next in importance beside them, and the ordering radiates outward, so the picture is a diagram of the organisation that anybody in it can read. Disputes about placement are common and are settled before the exposure. Height dictates the back. Taller people go behind, which is practical and produces a secondary effect: the arrangement partly sorts by physical characteristic rather than by anything meaningful, and readers of old photographs sometimes mistake position for standing. Symmetry does the rest. The group is balanced about a vertical axis, edges are kept even, and the whole occupies the frame with a margin, which produces the characteristic look that makes such photographs recognisable at a glance regardless of period. What the format finally records is a moment when a group existed. Many such photographs outlive every person in them and every institution they depict, and they are consulted afterwards for exactly the information the conventions encode — who was there, and where each of them stood. The photographer is almost never in it. Somebody stood behind the camera for every one of these pictures, and their absence from the record they made is so ordinary that nobody remarks on it. Group photographs of photographers are correspondingly rare.

subject: 간판과 상호의 서체
title: What a shop name is trying to say
content: A shop sign carries a name, and the choice of name and the way it is written together announce what kind of business waits inside. Both decisions are made by proprietors rather than by designers in most cases, and the resulting conventions are folk practice rather than professional design. Names cluster by trade. Certain words recur across shops of one kind — characters meaning abundance, longevity, or fortune for merchants, place names for restaurants claiming a regional cuisine, family names for businesses claiming continuity — so a passer-by classifies a shop before reading the whole sign. These conventions are strong enough that departing from them is a deliberate statement. The writing carries a second message. A name rendered in a formal calligraphic hand claims tradition and seriousness; the same name in a rounded modern letterform claims approachability; the same name in imported script claims something else again. Proprietors choose knowingly, and the choice frequently mismatches the actual age of the business. Materials add a third layer. Carved and painted wood, cut metal, moulded plastic, and illuminated boxes each signal an era and a price, and streets show all of them at once, so the visual record of a district's commercial history is legible in the accumulated signs. Older shops frequently keep a sign long past its material's fashion. Regulation shapes what is possible. Cities restrict size, projection, illumination, and sometimes language, and districts designated as historic impose further rules, so what appears on a street is a negotiation between what proprietors want and what authorities permit. Photographs from before such regulation show considerably more variety and considerably more chaos. Shops keep old signs for a reason. A worn board that has hung for forty years says something a new one cannot buy, so proprietors repaint rather than replace, and a street of such signs records how long each business has stood there.

subject: 벽보와 공공 소통
title: Notices pasted where everybody passes
content: Before broadcast media, reaching a whole community meant putting something on a wall where people walked. Official orders, trade notices, political appeals, and private messages all used the same wall, and the practice made a visual culture that survives mainly in photographs. The location did the targeting. A notice pasted at a market, a gate, or a crossroads reached whoever passed there, so posting sites were chosen for traffic, and authorities designated official boards while everybody else used whatever wall was available. Competition for the best positions was continuous. Format followed reading distance. Text meant to be read while walking is set large with few words; text for somebody who stops can be dense, and the two kinds look plainly different. Official notices tend toward density because readers were expected to stop, while commercial ones tend toward brevity. Layering is the medium's characteristic feature. New notices go over old ones, walls accumulate depth, and the resulting surface records a sequence, so researchers examining preserved fragments can reconstruct what was posted and when. Weather and overpasting destroy almost everything, which is why so little survives. Control of the wall was contested. Authorities licensed posting, tore down what they disliked, and charged those who pasted without leave, while movements shut out of other channels used walls because nobody could bar them, so a wall in a time of conflict is a record of it. Digital channels replaced the function and not the practice. Walls in many places still carry notices for audiences that other media do not reach — local services, missing animals, community events — which suggests the medium survives wherever a message needs to find people by where they walk rather than by who they are. Paper and paste were all it took. Anybody with a brush and a bucket could reach a whole district overnight, which is why walls have been used by every side in every conflict, and why authorities have always tried to control who owns them.

subject: 극장 건축과 음향
title: Building a room that carries a voice
content: A theatre must let an unamplified voice reach every seat while keeping the audience close enough to see a face. These two requirements pull against each other, and the history of theatre architecture is largely a record of compromises between them. Ancient open-air theatres solved it with geometry. A steep semicircular bank of stone seating focuses sound from a small area at its centre, the hard surfaces reflect rather than absorb, and the rising slope keeps every row in line of sight, so a voice from the performing area reaches the back rows with startling clarity. Measurements at surviving sites confirm what visitors report. Enclosed theatres introduced reverberation. A roof and walls return sound after a delay, which strengthens a voice and blurs consonants if the delay is long, so the shape of the room determines whether speech is supported or smeared. The horseshoe form with tiers of boxes, developed for opera, breaks up reflections while bringing many people close to the stage. Materials matter as much as shape. Wood resonates and reinforces, plaster reflects, and heavy fabric absorbs, so a theatre's sound changes when it is refurbished, and audiences have noticed and complained about renovations that altered acoustics unintentionally. An empty house sounds different from a full one, since bodies absorb. Amplification changed the calculation and not the problem. Sound systems permit any shape and any size, and they also flatten the difference between a live voice and a reproduced one, so theatres built for unamplified performance are now valued for exactly the quality that the technology made unnecessary. Companies working in them describe the room as a collaborator. Seats have never been equal. Some parts of any house hear better than others, the difference is large, and pricing has followed sound as much as sight for as long as tickets have been sold. Regular listeners learn where the good seats are.

subject: 무성 영화의 자막
title: Words on cards between the pictures
content: Films made before synchronised sound carried their dialogue and narration on cards inserted between shots. These were not a limitation reluctantly accepted but a component that studios designed, wrote, and occasionally rewrote after a film was finished, and the craft around them was substantial. Their number was a matter of judgement. Too many interrupted the flow and too few left audiences lost, and directors differed sharply, with some working to minimise them as a point of principle and others treating them as a resource. A few celebrated films used almost none, which required the visual storytelling to carry everything. The writing was specialised. Cards had to be readable in the time they were on screen, which limited them to a line or two, and the language was compressed accordingly, so writing them became a distinct occupation with its own practitioners. Studios employed people whose only job was this. Design carried tone. Cards were framed with borders, illustrated, and lettered in typefaces chosen for the film's genre, and comedies used ornament that dramas avoided, so the card announced what kind of film it belonged to before the words were read. Some productions changed the design between scenes. Translation was trivially easy, which mattered commercially. Replacing the cards adapted a film for any market at negligible cost, so films circulated internationally with a freedom that sound removed overnight, and studios shooting the same picture in several languages after the transition were solving a problem that had not existed. The form is occasionally revived. Directors who use cards in sound films rely on an audience that recognises the convention, which indicates that a technique abandoned a century ago remains legible. Musicians played in the room. A pianist or a small band followed the picture live, watching the screen and choosing from a stock of cues, so no two showings sounded alike and the same film varied from town to town.

subject: 화장의 문화적 문법
title: What painting a face is understood to mean
content: Changing the face with colour appears in nearly every culture, and what it means varies so widely that no single account covers it. It has marked rank, trade, ritual state, mourning, feasting, and availability, at times in one society at different moments. Ceremonial marking is the oldest documented use. Pigments recovered from burials and depicted in early art indicate faces painted for occasions rather than daily, and the patterns applied were prescribed by the occasion, so the practice functioned as a costume for the face rather than as enhancement. Several traditions retain exactly this use. Daily cosmetic use developed separately and carries different meanings. Where it became ordinary, rules grew up about how much suits whom and when, and those rules carry age, marriage, trade, and standing, so a face that departs from them says something whether or not anybody meant it to. The stuff used records trade and craft. Mineral pigments, plant dyes, and later synthetic compounds each left evidence, and several widely used preparations were poisonous — lead-based whiteners in particular caused documented harm across centuries — which indicates how strong the social requirement was. Theatrical use is a distinct tradition. Stage makeup exaggerates for distance and lighting rather than for close viewing, and in traditions using fixed character types the patterns identify the role, so a knowledgeable audience reads the face as a name. These conventions are taught and vary by tradition. Regulation appears repeatedly. Authorities in many periods restricted who might paint their face and how, which is a reliable indicator that the practice was understood to make claims about standing rather than merely about appearance. Men wore it too in many periods. Painted faces at court, on stage, and in mourning were ordinary for men across several centuries, and the idea that the practice belongs to one sex is recent and local rather than general.

subject: 공원이라는 발명
title: Setting aside land for people to walk in
content: A public park is a piece of city left unbuilt on purpose for common use, and the idea is younger than most people think. Royal hunting grounds and private gardens existed for centuries; land reserved by a municipality for anybody to enter is a nineteenth century development in most countries. The argument for them was medical before it was recreational. Reformers held that crowded working districts lacked air and light, that sickness followed, and that open ground would help, so the first town parks were argued for in just those terms and were often placed where the need was worst. The reasoning was partly mistaken and the conclusion was sound. Design followed a specific aesthetic. Winding paths, loose planting, made lakes, and clumps of trees set with care come from a garden tradition built for country estates, so what a town dweller met was a squeezed version of gentry scenery. Straight avenues and formal beds appeared where a different tradition dominated. Rules governed conduct from the beginning. Keeping off the grass, restrictions on games, hours of opening, and prohibitions on various activities appeared alongside the parks themselves, so the space was public and supervised, and disputes about what may be done there have continued ever since. Provision was never even. Parks were placed where land was available and where influential residents wanted them, so the distribution across a city rarely matched the need that justified them, and studies of many cities find that pattern persisting into the present. Recent movements have concentrated on exactly this inequality rather than on creating new parks in places that already have several. Trees take longer than governments. A park planted now looks thin for thirty years and settles into what its designer intended long after they are dead, so the work asks for a patience that few public projects are given.

subject: 기념품이 하는 일
title: Objects bought to prove you were somewhere
content: A souvenir is purchased at a place, carries little use value, and functions afterwards as evidence and as a trigger for memory. The trade in such objects is old, and the forms it takes reveal what travellers wanted from the places they visited. Portability determined the type. Objects had to survive a journey and fit in a bag, so the trade favoured small, durable, and light things, and the categories that recur across centuries — miniature models, images, containers, and items of dress — reflect that constraint rather than any local tradition. Pilgrimage badges are the earliest well documented form. Authenticity is negotiated rather than given. Buyers want something of the place, sellers supply what buyers want, and the resulting objects range from genuine local products to items manufactured elsewhere and labelled locally. Studies of tourist markets consistently find that what sells is what matches visitors' expectations of a place rather than what residents actually use. Craft traditions adapt to the trade. Where visitors buy handmade objects, production shifts toward what sells — smaller, brighter, faster to make — and this has been documented as both preserving crafts that would otherwise have ended and altering them beyond what practitioners intended. Both outcomes are usually present in the same tradition. The object works by association afterwards. Its value is entirely in what it recalls, which is why souvenirs are meaningless to anybody but their owner and are discarded when that owner dies, and why the same object bought at home would carry nothing. What is being purchased is a claim about having been somewhere, and the object is merely where the claim is stored. Most of them end up in a drawer. Objects bought to hold a memory are looked at for a season and then stored, and their eventual fate is a house clearance, which is why so few survive from any period despite the numbers made.

subject: 간판 글씨의 서체
title: Letters painted by somebody who never trained as a designer
content: Hand-painted commercial lettering forms a tradition transmitted between practitioners rather than through schools, and its conventions differ region by region in ways that specialists identify at a glance. The trade has largely ended, and its documentation began late. Brush behaviour shapes the letterforms. A loaded brush drawn along a surface produces a stroke that thickens and thins according to pressure and angle, so the shapes that result differ fundamentally from those a designer draws and a machine cuts. Sign painters learned to exploit this rather than to fight it, which is why hand lettering has a rhythm that reproduction lacks. Speed was a commercial requirement. A painter charged by the job and worked at height in weather, so techniques favoured strokes that could be laid confidently in one pass, and the characteristic forms of the trade are those that a practised hand produces quickly. Hesitation shows immediately in the line. Layout was done by eye. Spacing letters so that a word reads evenly is a judgement rather than a measurement, since identical gaps between letters look uneven, and painters developed this judgement over years without ever expressing it numerically. Software now does the same job by rule and produces results that specialists identify as mechanical. Apprenticeship transmitted everything. A beginner mixed paint, prepared surfaces, and watched for years before lettering anything visible, and the whole body of knowledge lived in that relationship, so the trade's decline removed it within a generation. Recent revivals have reconstructed the techniques from surviving practitioners and from manuals, which is possible and slow, and the practitioners involved describe recovering the hand as taking far longer than learning the rules. The trade had its own words. Painters named their brushes, their strokes, and their faults in terms that outsiders never heard, and much of that vocabulary went with the practitioners, so recovering it has meant interviewing the few who are left.

subject: 무대 분장의 기법
title: Painting a face to be seen from the back row
content: Stage makeup solves a problem that has nothing to do with everyday cosmetics. Strong overhead lighting flattens features and washes out colour, and the audience sits too far away to see detail, so the face must be rebuilt to read at distance under conditions that erase it. Lighting is the enemy. Illumination from above deepens the eye sockets and casts the nose downward, so makeup counteracts what the lights do, adding colour where the light removes it and shadow where the light flattens. A face made up correctly for the stage looks alarming in ordinary light, which performers find disconcerting until they see it from the auditorium. Distance sets the scale. Everything is exaggerated in proportion to how far the furthest seat sits, so a small theatre requires far less than a large one, and a performer moving between houses adjusts accordingly. Film reversed the requirement entirely, since a camera close to the face shows every edge. Character work is a separate craft. Ageing, altering features, and building prosthetic pieces require different materials and considerably more time, and the specialists who do this work in film and theatre train separately from those doing straight makeup. Traditions using fixed character types prescribe patterns exactly. Several theatrical traditions apply painted patterns that identify a role by colour and design, so an audience reads the character before the performer speaks, and the patterns are learned rather than invented. Practitioners in those traditions apply their own makeup as part of preparing for the role, and describe the process as where the performance begins. Sweat is the standing problem. Stage lighting is hot, a performer works hard, and everything applied must survive two hours of it, so the craft is as much about what stays put as about what it looks like when first applied.

subject: 악기 조율사의 귀
title: Tuning by listening to what is not there
content: A piano tuner does not set each string to a measured frequency. They listen to the interference between two notes sounded together — a pulsing that speeds up as the interval moves away from pure — and adjust until that pulsing occurs at the rate the tuning requires. The technique is counting a sound that neither string is making. The pulsing is unavoidable in equal temperament. Because the system requires every interval except the octave to be slightly impure, a tuner is deliberately introducing error, and the skill lies in distributing it so that no key sounds worse than another. A tuner who eliminated the pulsing entirely in one interval would ruin several others. The sequence matters. Tuning begins with a reference note, proceeds through a set of intervals within one octave to establish the temperament, and then extends outward by octaves, so an error early in the sequence propagates through the whole instrument. Experienced tuners check back repeatedly against earlier notes. Stretching is required by physics. Strings are not ideal, so their overtones lie slightly higher than theory predicts, and an instrument tuned to exact octaves sounds flat in the treble, which means tuners widen the octaves progressively toward both ends by an amount they judge by ear. Electronic devices now model this. The instrument fights back. Strings settle after being moved, so a tuner sets each slightly past its target and lets it return, and a piano tuned once will drift within weeks, which is why the work is periodic rather than permanent. Concert instruments are tuned before every performance and frequently during intervals. Weather moves the instrument. Wood swells and shrinks with damp, so a piano drifts with the seasons regardless of use, and a room kept at a steady humidity does more for tuning than any amount of skill at the pins.

subject: 악극과 대중 취향의 형성
title: Popular musical theatre and what audiences learned to want
content: Musical theatre made for a broad paying audience developed in several countries during the same decades, combining song, spoken scenes, comedy, and spectacle in proportions that varied by tradition. What such shows accomplished was training an audience in what to expect from an evening's entertainment. The form was assembled from what already worked. Songs that had sold as sheet music, comic routines from variety stages, and plots borrowed from popular fiction were combined, so the shows were compilations before they were compositions, and the earliest examples were revised continuously according to what audiences responded to. Commercial feedback shaped the material directly. Structure settled into a pattern. An opening establishing the situation, songs at emotional peaks, comic relief between them, and a large ensemble number before the close became standard, and audiences learned to anticipate each element, so a show departing from the sequence was experienced as odd rather than as original. The pattern persists in musical theatre now. Music was written to be taken away. Songs were built to be memorable on one hearing and singable by amateurs, since sheet music sales were a substantial part of a production's income, and this requirement shaped melodic range, phrase length, and harmonic simplicity. A song too difficult to sing at home earned less. The tradition shaped taste beyond the theatre. Audiences trained on these conventions brought them to radio, to film, and to recorded music, so the expectations established in a commercial theatre determined what a whole century of popular music was measured against, which is a considerable influence for a form that critics of the period dismissed as trivial. The shows were made to travel. Companies took a successful production from town to town for years, adapting it to each house, so a work existed as many versions rather than one, and no printed script records what audiences actually saw.
